rv.q: “They carried Floyd right on up in the sky,” Vera, his on-again, off-again girlfriend, says of the mysterious men dressed in black who’d turned up at the cemetery. “That go to show you I don’t know too much about nothing,” replies Red Carter, one of the deceased’s acolytes.

Though Santiago-Hudson doesn't pull off a production that keeps that engine consistently blazing, he — as a superb actor of Wilson himself — does make space for us to meet these people in all their fullness. And that's not nothing.
Like a great blues composition, Seven Guitars finds beauty in sorrow, humor in hardship and poetry in pain.

He has also smartly enlisted blues guitarist Junior Mack (they worked together in Santiago-Hudson's solo play Lackawanna Blues a few years back) to provide original music to accompany what is a richly rewarding production.
Director Ruben Santiago-Hudson’s connection to August Wilson is evident in this deeply intimate, leisurely, and strong 30th-anniversary revival of Seven Guitars.
Santiago-Hudson has assembled an ensemble full of Wilsonian actors that could hardly be bettered
Wilson’s lyrical feel for Black-American life is enough of a special effect in and of itself.
In their characters’ varied reactions to the rooster crowing in a neighbor’s backyard, a cast of seven exemplary performers illuminates Black life in the Hill District of Pittsburgh in 1948
Santiago-Hudson presents us a haunting production that’s not just absorbing, charged, and emotional but one that brings music to a level I have never seen before in a play.
The director has delivered a masterpiece, a sizzling, emotionally rich revival with perfect casting that constantly crackles with life.
This production is so insightful and razor sharp in its messages.
As in any blues number, Seven Guitars succeeds on the strength of an ensemble that blends well even as it astonishes us with its sudden variations.
August Wilson’s Seven Guitars begins at a graveside yet makes room for bawdy laughs, unrequited love, and a bluesman who refuses to live his life without.

cn.t: Wilson's *Seven Guitars* earns strong praise in this Lincoln Center revival, with most critics lauding Santiago-Hudson's direction and the ensemble cast. A few find the play itself uneven, but all agree the production brings Wilson's blues-infused poetry vividly to life.
